what_it_does: Modern CPUs use a hierarchy of memory: a small, very fast on-chip cache, and then large but slower off-chip DRAM (Dynamic Random-Access Memory). A popular trick is to use a layer of high-bandwidth memory — such as HBM3 (High Bandwidth Memory version 3), a stacked chip that sits very close to the processor — as a large intermediate cache. The problem is that every cache lookup requires two sequential steps: first fetch the 'tag' (a small label identifying what data is stored in that cache slot) and then, only if it matches, fetch the actual data. This two-step dance wastes time and bandwidth. TDRAM (Tag-enhanced DRAM) adds a small section of low-latency metadata storage directly onto the HBM3 chip, right next to the main data arrays. This lets the chip start reading both the tag and the data in parallel (like unlocking a door and pushing it open at the same time), compare the tag internally, and send the data to the CPU only if the tag matched — avoiding any wasted data transfer when the data is not what the CPU wanted. An additional 'flush buffer' inside the chip handles the awkward case where a write miss forces a dirty (modified) old value to be written back before new data can be fetched, eliminating the dead time on the data bus during that transition.
